name: SQL Fundamentals
description: The queries that show up in every technical screen.
intro: SQL is the language used to pull and shape data out of a database, and it shows up constantly in technical screens for data, finance, and analyst roles, sometimes as a live coding exercise, sometimes as a question about how a query would behave. If you have never written a query before, that is completely normal at this stage: this deck starts from what a table and a query actually are, then builds up to the join types and grouping logic interviewers actually test. Think of it less as memorizing syntax and more as learning to read a data question and know which SQL concept it is really asking about.

cards.q: What’s the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?
cards.takeaway: INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless.
cards.a: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have a match in both tables, dropping anything without a corresponding row on either side. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left (first) table no matter what, filling in NULLs for the right table's columns wherever no match exists. Reach for LEFT JOIN when you need to preserve every record from your main table, like every customer, even the ones who haven't placed an order yet.

cards.q: What does GROUP BY actually do, and why do non-aggregated columns need to be in it?
cards.takeaway: GROUP BY folds rows that share a value into one summary row per group.
cards.a: GROUP BY collapses every row that shares the same value in one or more columns into a single summary row, which is what lets aggregate functions like SUM, COUNT, or AVG operate on each group instead of the whole table. Any column in the SELECT list that isn't wrapped in an aggregate has to be listed in GROUP BY too, because once hundreds of rows fold into one, the database needs a rule for which single value to display.

cards.q: What’s the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
cards.takeaway: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping.
cards.a: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, so it has no concept yet of an aggregate like SUM(sales). HAVING runs after GROUP BY, filtering the resulting groups instead of raw rows, which is why it's the clause you'd reach for to say something like “only show regions where total sales exceed $1M.”

cards.q: What can a window function do that a plain GROUP BY can’t?
cards.takeaway: Window functions add a calculated column to every row instead of collapsing rows into groups.
cards.a: A window function, like SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ...), calculates an aggregate across a set of related rows without collapsing anything: every original row survives, with the calculated value added alongside it. That's what makes a running total, a rank within each category, or a moving average possible, none of which a plain GROUP BY can produce, since GROUP BY always reduces many rows down to one.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
cards.takeaway: A primary key is unique to its own table; a foreign key points to a primary key in another table.
cards.a: A primary key uniquely identifies each row within its own table: no two rows can share one, and it can never be NULL. A foreign key is a column in one table that references a primary key in another table, and that reference is how relational databases enforce that a relationship, like an order pointing to a real, existing customer, actually holds up.

cards.q: How would you find duplicate rows in a table?
cards.takeaway: Group by the columns that should be unique, then filter for groups with more than one row.
cards.a: Group the table by whichever columns are supposed to be unique, count how many rows land in each group with COUNT(*), then filter with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Whatever groups survive that filter are your duplicates, rows that shouldn't have more than one match but do.

cards.q: What does COALESCE do?
cards.takeaway: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value in a list, handy for fallback defaults.
cards.a: COALESCE takes a list of values and returns the first one that isn't NULL. That makes it a clean way to supply a fallback: for example, COALESCE(discount, 0) treats a missing discount as zero instead of letting a NULL silently break a calculation further down the query.

cards.q: What’s the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
cards.takeaway: UNION removes duplicate rows when combining results; UNION ALL keeps every row, duplicates included.
cards.a: Both UNION and UNION ALL stack the results of two queries into one combined result set. UNION additionally removes any duplicate rows, which takes an extra sort-and-compare step, while UNION ALL keeps every row exactly as it came, duplicates included, and runs faster because it skips that de-duplication work.

cards.q: How do you calculate a running total in SQL?
cards.takeaway: A window function adds a cumulative sum column without collapsing or reordering any rows.
cards.a: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) adds up the amount column cumulatively as it moves through the rows in date order. It produces a new running-total column sitting right alongside the original data, without collapsing or reordering any of the underlying rows.

name: Reading Financial Statements
description: How the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement fit together.
intro: Every finance and consulting interview eventually touches the three financial statements, the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, because they are how a business actually gets described in numbers. This deck is built for someone who has never opened a company’s annual report: it walks through what each statement shows, why they exist as three separate documents instead of one, and how a single transaction ripples across all three. By the end, you should be able to hear "walk me through the financial statements" and actually enjoy answering it.

cards.q: What are the three core financial statements, and how do they connect?
cards.takeaway: Net income is the thread that stitches the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement together.
cards.a: The income statement shows profitability over a period: revenue minus expenses equals net income. The balance sheet is a snapshot of what the company owns and owes at one specific moment, assets, liabilities, and equity. The cash flow statement tracks how cash actually moved during that same period. Net income is what ties them together: it flows into the cash flow statement's starting line and into retained earnings on the balance sheet.

cards.q: What’s the key difference between the balance sheet and the income statement in terms of time?
cards.takeaway: The income statement covers a stretch of time; the balance sheet freezes one exact moment.
cards.a: The income statement covers a period, a quarter or a year, showing what happened over that stretch. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one exact moment, showing what the company owns and owes as of that date. Think of it like the difference between a video and a photo: one captures a stretch of activity, the other captures a single instant.

cards.q: What is working capital, and how is it calculated?
cards.takeaway: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, a quick read on short-term liquidity.
cards.a: Working capital measures how easily a company can cover its near-term obligations: current assets minus current liabilities. A positive number means the company has enough short-term assets, cash, receivables, inventory, to meet what it owes in the near future. A shrinking or negative figure is often an early warning sign of cash flow trouble ahead.

cards.q: Why can cash flow and net income diverge, even in the same period?
cards.takeaway: Net income books revenue the moment it's earned; cash flow only counts money that's actually landed.
cards.a: Net income includes non-cash items like depreciation, and under accrual accounting it counts revenue as soon as it's earned, not when the cash actually arrives. Cash flow only counts money that has physically moved. That's why a company can show a healthy profit on paper while its cash balance falls, if customers haven't paid yet or cash is tied up sitting in inventory.

cards.q: What are the three sections of the cash flow statement?
cards.takeaway: Operating, investing, and financing activities add up to explain exactly why cash changed.
cards.a: Operating activities capture cash generated or used by the core business. Investing activities cover cash spent on or received from things like equipment or acquisitions. Financing activities capture cash from debt, equity raises, dividends, or buybacks. Add all three together and you get the full explanation for why the cash balance changed over the period.

cards.q: How does depreciation affect the income statement differently than the cash flow statement?
cards.takeaway: Depreciation cuts net income as an expense, then gets added straight back on the cash flow statement.
cards.a: Depreciation reduces net income on the income statement because it's recorded as an expense, even though no cash actually leaves the business that period. On the cash flow statement, it gets added back in the operating section, since that statement's whole job is to reflect real cash movement, not accounting expense.

cards.q: What is the accounting equation?
cards.takeaway: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity, everything owned was funded by debt or by owners.
cards.a: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Everything a company owns, its assets, was funded either by borrowing (liabilities) or by owners' investment and retained profit (equity). The balance sheet has to balance to this equation at all times, which is exactly where its name comes from.

cards.q: What does accrual accounting mean, and how is it different from cash accounting?
cards.takeaway: Accrual accounting counts revenue when it's earned, not when the cash actually shows up.
cards.a: Accrual accounting records revenue when it's earned and expenses when they're incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands, so a sale made on credit counts as revenue immediately. Cash accounting only records a transaction once cash physically moves. Most real companies use accrual accounting because it matches revenue to the period it was actually generated in, giving a truer picture of performance.

cards.q: What is EBITDA, and why do analysts use it?
cards.takeaway: EBITDA adds interest, taxes, and D&A back to net income to isolate pure operating performance.
cards.a: EBITDA stands for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, essentially operating profit before the effects of financing decisions and non-cash accounting charges. Analysts use it to compare operating performance across companies with different capital structures or tax situations, since it strips those differences away and leaves the core business result.

name: Valuation Basics
description: DCF, comps, and the multiples analysts actually use.
intro: Valuation is the skill of putting a number on what a company or investment is actually worth, and it is one of the most commonly tested topics in finance interviews, from "walk me through a DCF" to "how would you value this company." This deck introduces the core methods, discounted cash flow, comparable companies, and the multiples analysts lean on, in plain language first, then in the more technical form interviewers expect. No prior valuation experience assumed, just a willingness to think in terms of cash flow and comparison.

cards.q: What is a DCF, and why do we discount future cash flows?
cards.takeaway: A DCF says a company is worth all the cash it will ever generate, brought back to today's dollars.
cards.a: You forecast the company's free cash flow for the next several years, then discount each year back to present value using a discount rate (usually WACC), since a dollar next year is worth less than a dollar today: it carries risk, and that same dollar could be earning a return elsewhere. Add those discounted years together, plus a terminal value for everything beyond the forecast window, and that sum is today's value.

cards.q: What is WACC, and what does it represent?
cards.takeaway: WACC is the blended cost of a company's money, part debt, part equity.
cards.a: Every company funds itself with some mix of debt and equity, and each has a cost: debt costs interest (though it's tax-deductible, making it effectively cheaper than its stated rate), equity costs the return shareholders expect. WACC blends those two costs, weighted by how much of each the company actually uses. It's used as the DCF's discount rate because it represents the minimum return the company's investments need to clear to be worth funding.

cards.q: What is “terminal value” in a DCF?
cards.takeaway: Terminal value covers everything a business earns after the forecast period ends.
cards.a: A DCF only forecasts in detail for about 5–10 years, but the company is assumed to keep operating indefinitely beyond that. Terminal value estimates all of that remaining future in one lump sum, discounted back to today just like any other cash flow. It's typically the single largest piece of a DCF's total value, which is why the assumptions behind it (a long-run growth rate, or an exit multiple) matter so much.

cards.q: What is comparable company analysis (“comps”)?
cards.takeaway: Comps value a company by comparing it to similar public companies' current pricing.
cards.a: Instead of building a value from scratch like a DCF does, comps anchor to what the market is already paying for similar businesses, typically using a ratio like EV/EBITDA or P/E, then apply that same multiple to the company being valued. It's a relative valuation method: quicker than a DCF, and it reflects real market sentiment, for better or worse.

cards.q: What does EV/EBITDA measure, and why use enterprise value instead of just market cap?
cards.takeaway: EV/EBITDA compares total company value to operating earnings, ignoring how the company is financed.
cards.a: Enterprise value is used instead of market cap because it also accounts for debt and cash, making it possible to compare companies fairly even when they have very different capital structures: market cap alone ignores how much of the business is funded by debt. EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) strips out financing and accounting choices, so you're comparing pure operating performance.

cards.q: What’s the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
cards.takeaway: Enterprise value is the whole business; equity value is just the shareholders' slice.
cards.a: Enterprise value represents the value of the whole business, what it would cost to acquire the company outright, including taking on its debt and stripping out its cash. Equity value is just the value belonging to shareholders (what market cap represents). The bridge between them: enterprise value = equity value + debt − cash.

cards.q: What is a P/E ratio, and what does a high P/E typically signal?
cards.takeaway: P/E shows how much investors pay today for each dollar the company currently earns.
cards.a: The price-to-earnings ratio divides a company's share price by its earnings per share. A high P/E usually signals that the market expects strong future earnings growth, since investors are willing to pay more today for the same current profit; in some cases it simply means the stock is overvalued relative to its fundamentals, so P/E alone doesn't tell you which story is true.

cards.q: What is precedent transactions analysis, and how does it differ from comps?
cards.takeaway: Precedent transactions value a company using prices actually paid in past M&A deals.
cards.a: Unlike comps, which look at how similar companies trade on public markets day-to-day, this method looks at what acquirers have actually paid to buy similar businesses outright. Because acquisitions usually include a control premium (extra paid to gain control of the company), precedent transaction multiples tend to run higher than trading comps.

cards.q: Why does a valuation usually get presented as a range (a “football field”) rather than a single number?
cards.takeaway: A valuation range, not one number, because every method rests on assumptions that can shift.
cards.a: Growth rates, discount rates, which comps are truly comparable: small changes in any of these assumptions can shift the output meaningfully. Presenting a range across multiple methods (DCF, comps, precedent transactions) is more honest about that uncertainty than pretending a single precise number is correct.

name: Excel & Data Analysis
description: The functions and habits behind a clean model.
intro: Excel is the quiet backbone of almost every business and finance role, and interviewers use it as a proxy for whether you can actually build and check a model, not just talk about one. This deck covers the functions, habits, and data-cleaning logic that come up again and again, pivot tables, lookups, and the kind of small decisions that separate a clean spreadsheet from a fragile one. If your Excel experience is mostly basic formulas so far, this is exactly the right starting point.

cards.q: What does a pivot table do?
cards.takeaway: A pivot table turns thousands of raw rows into a compact, instant summary grid.
cards.a: A pivot table summarizes a large dataset by letting you drag fields into rows, columns, and values, instantly regrouping and aggregating the data behind the scenes. That turns thousands of raw transaction-level rows into a compact summary, like total sales by region by month, without writing a single formula. Drag a different field into a different slot, and the whole summary reshapes itself instantly.

cards.q: What’s the difference between VLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH?
cards.takeaway: VLOOKUP only searches rightward from its first column; INDEX/MATCH can look either way.

INDEX/MATCH splits the job in two: MATCH finds the row position, and INDEX pulls the value from any column you point it to, left or right of the lookup column. cards.takeaway: Relative references shift when copied; a $ locks a reference to one fixed cell.
cards.a: A relative reference (like A1) automatically shifts to match its new position whenever the formula is copied elsewhere. An absolute reference (like $A$1) stays locked to that exact cell no matter where the formula goes. That's essential when a formula needs to keep pointing at one fixed value, like a tax rate or exchange rate stored in a single cell, while the rest of the formula moves normally.

cards.q: What is conditional formatting, and when is it useful?
cards.takeaway: Conditional formatting auto-styles cells by their value, so outliers jump out visually.
cards.a: Conditional formatting automatically changes a cell's appearance, color, font, or icon, based on rules applied to its value, like highlighting any expense over budget in red. It turns a plain grid of numbers into something you can scan visually, spotting outliers or exceptions immediately instead of reading every cell.

cards.q: What is data validation used for in a spreadsheet?
cards.takeaway: Data validation blocks bad entries at the source instead of cleaning them up later.
cards.a: Data validation restricts what can be entered into a cell, like a dropdown list, a number range, or a required date format. That prevents bad or inconsistent data from getting into a model in the first place, rather than having to clean it up after the fact.

cards.q: What can SUMIFS or COUNTIFS do that SUM or COUNT can’t?
cards.takeaway: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS add conditions that SUM and COUNT can't apply on their own.
cards.a: SUM and COUNT operate on an entire range with no conditions attached. SUMIFS and COUNTIFS let you sum or count only the rows that meet one or more criteria at once, for example, summing revenue only where the region is EMEA and the quarter is Q1, without needing a pivot table or a separately filtered copy of the data.

cards.q: What does “data cleaning” typically involve?
cards.takeaway: Data cleaning fixes a dataset's errors and inconsistencies before it gets analyzed.
cards.a: Data cleaning means fixing a dataset before analyzing it: removing duplicate rows, standardizing inconsistent formats (like “NY” vs “New York”), handling missing values, and correcting obvious errors. It matters because even a well-built model produces misleading output when the underlying data is inconsistent.

cards.q: What’s the difference between structured and unstructured data?
cards.takeaway: Structured data fits neat rows and columns; unstructured data has no predefined shape.
cards.a: Structured data fits neatly into rows and columns with a defined format, like a spreadsheet or a SQL table, which makes it easy to query and analyze directly. Unstructured data, emails, PDFs, images, free-text notes, has no predefined format and usually needs to be processed or extracted before it can be analyzed the same way. Most real-world data work has to handle both.

cards.q: What is a “helper column,” and why use one?
cards.takeaway: A helper column breaks a messy formula into simple, checkable intermediate steps.
cards.a: A helper column is an extra column added purely to break a complex calculation into a simpler intermediate step. It's not part of the final output; it's there to make a formula easier to build, audit, and debug, rather than cramming all the logic into one unreadable nested formula.

name: Corporate Finance & Investment Basics
description: Time value of money, NPV, IRR, and how companies decide where to put capital.
intro: This deck is about how companies actually decide where to put their money, using ideas like the time value of money, net present value, and internal rate of return. These concepts sound abstract until you realize interviewers use them to test whether you can reason about a decision the way a finance team actually would. Expect a mix of "what does this term mean" and "how would you use it to make a call," both of which come up in real interviews.

cards.q: What is the time value of money, and why does it matter?
cards.takeaway: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can already be earning a return.
cards.a: Money in hand today is worth more than the same amount later, because it can be invested right away to start earning a return, and because inflation and risk chip away at what a future dollar can actually buy. This is the foundational idea behind discounting, NPV, and virtually every valuation method: you can't compare a dollar today to a dollar in five years without adjusting for that gap.

cards.q: What is Net Present Value (NPV), and how is it used to decide on a project?
cards.takeaway: NPV converts a project's future cash flows into today's dollars and nets out what it cost to get started.
cards.a: NPV takes a project's expected future cash flows, discounts each one back to present value using the company's cost of capital, and adds them all up. Then it subtracts the initial investment, leaving the net value the project is actually expected to create. The decision rule follows directly: accept projects with a positive NPV, since they're expected to earn more than the cost of capital, and reject the ones with a negative NPV.

cards.q: What is the Internal Rate of Return (IRR)?
cards.takeaway: IRR is the discount rate that makes a project's NPV exactly zero, its own break-even return.
cards.a: IRR is the discount rate at which a project's NPV works out to exactly zero, so it's essentially the project's built-in break-even rate of return. To decide if a project is worth doing, compare its IRR against the company's required rate of return, or hurdle rate: if the IRR clears that hurdle, the project is generally worth pursuing.

cards.q: What is the payback period, and what's its main limitation?
cards.takeaway: Payback period tells you how fast you get your money back, but ignores everything after that.
cards.a: The payback period is simply how long it takes for a project's cumulative cash flows to add back up to the initial investment. Its main blind spot is that it ignores the time value of money, treating a dollar in year one the same as a dollar in year four, and it ignores any cash flows that happen after the payback point. That's why it's usually used alongside NPV or IRR rather than as a stand-alone decision tool.

cards.q: What is capital structure?
cards.takeaway: Capital structure is just the mix of debt and equity a company uses to fund itself.
cards.a: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity a company uses to fund its operations and growth. That mix matters because it shapes the company's cost of capital, risk, and flexibility: debt is generally cheaper and doesn't dilute ownership, but it comes with fixed repayment obligations regardless of how the business performs, while equity carries no repayment obligation but costs more and dilutes existing owners.

cards.q: What is the difference between a bond and a stock, at a basic level?
cards.takeaway: A bond is a loan with a promised repayment; a stock is ownership with no promises either way.
cards.a: A bond is essentially a loan: an investor gives a company or government money, and in return it promises to pay back the principal plus periodic interest (coupons) on a fixed schedule. A stock is different: it represents partial ownership in a company, with no promised repayment at all. Its value simply depends on the company's future performance and however the market chooses to price that.

cards.q: What does "cost of capital" mean, intuitively?
cards.takeaway: Cost of capital is the minimum return a company must earn on anything it invests in, or it's destroying value.
cards.a: Cost of capital is the return a company has to offer to attract funding, whether that's interest paid to lenders (cost of debt) or the return shareholders expect (cost of equity), and it rises with how risky investors perceive the company to be. Think of it as a hurdle rate: any project or investment the company takes on needs to earn more than this just to be worth doing.

cards.q: What is diversification, and why does it reduce risk?
cards.takeaway: Diversification spreads money across assets that don't all move together, smoothing out the bumps.
cards.a: Diversification means spreading your money across multiple assets whose returns don't move in lockstep, so when one investment dips, others are likely holding steady or gaining, cushioning the blow. Because different assets react differently to the same events, a diversified portfolio typically ends up with lower overall volatility than any single holding inside it.

cards.q: What is the difference between systematic and unsystematic risk?
cards.takeaway: Systematic risk hits the whole market and can't be diversified away; unsystematic risk is company-specific and can.
cards.a: Systematic risk is market-wide, things like interest rate moves or a recession, and it affects nearly every asset at once, so no amount of diversification eliminates it. Unsystematic risk is specific to a single company or industry, like a product recall or a lawsuit, and this is the risk diversification actually protects against: spread your holdings widely enough, and one asset's specific problems just get absorbed by the others.

name: Statistics & Data Analysis for Business
description: The core statistical concepts behind sound, defensible business analysis.
intro: Most business and data roles do not expect you to be a statistician, but they do expect you to reason clearly about numbers: what an average actually tells you, when a sample might be misleading, how confident you can really be in a conclusion. This deck focuses on the statistical concepts that come up in business contexts specifically, not abstract math theory, so the framing stays close to how you would actually use it in an interview or on the job. No statistics background required to start.

cards.q: What’s the difference between mean, median, and mode, and when does it matter which one you use?
cards.takeaway: Mean is the average, median is the middle, mode is the most common — skewed data favors the median.
cards.a: Mean adds up every value and divides by the count, median is the middle value once everything's sorted, and mode is whichever value shows up most often. The choice matters because the mean gets dragged around by outliers — a few extreme values can pull it far from what's typical — while the median holds steady and better represents a “typical” case in skewed data, like income or home prices.

cards.q: What’s the difference between correlation and causation?
cards.takeaway: Two variables moving together doesn't mean one causes the other — a hidden third factor might explain both.
cards.a: Correlation just means two variables tend to move together; it doesn't prove that one causes the other. There could be a hidden third factor driving both, or the pattern could be pure coincidence. Causation means a change in one variable actually produces the change in the other, and proving that usually takes a controlled experiment or careful statistical work, not just an observed pattern.

cards.q: What is a p-value, in plain terms?
cards.takeaway: A p-value is the odds you'd see a result this extreme if nothing real were actually going on.
cards.a: A p-value estimates the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as what you observed, assuming there's actually no real effect. The smaller the p-value, the less likely that outcome is to be pure chance — below 0.05 is the common cutoff, which is why it's used as the threshold for calling a result “statistically significant.”

cards.q: What is a confidence interval?
cards.takeaway: A confidence interval is a range of plausible values, not a single guess — it expresses how much uncertainty surrounds an estimate.
cards.a: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for something you don't know exactly — like a population average — built from your sample data, rather than one single point estimate. A 95% confidence interval means that if you repeated the same sampling process many times, about 95% of the intervals you'd construct would contain the true value. It's a way of expressing uncertainty around an estimate, not a guarantee about any one specific interval.

cards.q: What is regression analysis used for?
cards.takeaway: Regression puts a number on how much an outcome changes when an input changes.
cards.a: Regression analysis estimates the relationship between an outcome (the dependent variable) and one or more factors that might explain it (the independent variables), letting you put a number on how much the outcome shifts as an input changes. In business it's used constantly — forecasting sales, estimating what pricing or marketing spend actually does to revenue, and figuring out which factors matter most in predicting an outcome.

cards.q: What is A/B testing?
cards.takeaway: A/B testing randomly splits an audience into two groups to fairly compare which version performs better.
cards.a: A/B testing compares two versions of something — a webpage, an email subject line — by randomly assigning different users to each version and measuring which one wins on a defined metric. Randomization is what makes the comparison fair: it ensures the two groups are alike in every way except the one thing you're testing, so any difference in outcome can be attributed to that change.

cards.q: What is sample bias, and why is it a problem?
cards.takeaway: Sample bias means your data doesn't represent the population you're trying to understand, so conclusions don't generalize.
cards.a: Sample bias happens when the data you collect isn't actually representative of the population you're trying to draw conclusions about, so whatever you learn from it doesn't generalize. A classic example is surveying only your existing customers about a new product idea — you'd completely miss the opinions of everyone who looked at what you offer and decided not to buy.

cards.q: What’s the difference between descriptive and predictive analytics?
cards.takeaway: Descriptive analytics explains what already happened; predictive analytics forecasts what's likely to happen next.
cards.a: Descriptive analytics summarizes what has already happened — like last quarter's sales broken out by region. Predictive analytics goes further, using patterns in that historical data to estimate what's likely to happen next, like forecasting next quarter's numbers. Most business analysis starts descriptive, establishing a clear picture of the past, before it moves on to prediction.

name: Management & Strategy Frameworks
description: The core frameworks used to analyze markets, competitors, and business decisions.
intro: Case interviews and strategy conversations lean heavily on a small set of well-known frameworks, SWOT, Porter’s five forces, the kind of tools that give structure to a messy business question. This deck introduces each one from scratch: what it is for, when it actually applies, and the trap of using it as a checklist instead of a thinking tool. If you have never used a strategy framework before, this is designed to get you comfortable enough to reach for the right one under pressure.

cards.q: What is a SWOT analysis?
cards.takeaway: SWOT sorts a company's position into internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.
cards.a: SWOT is a simple four-box way to take stock of where a company stands before making a strategic call. Strengths and weaknesses are internal, things the company controls, like its brand or cost structure, while opportunities and threats come from the external environment, like market trends or new competitors. Laying all four out side by side helps surface what to build on, what to fix, what to chase, and what to defend against.

cards.q: What are Porter’s Five Forces?
cards.takeaway: Five surrounding pressures, rivals, entrants, substitutes, and supplier/buyer power, decide how profitable an industry can be.
cards.a: Porter's Five Forces size up how attractive an industry actually is, based on five competitive pressures bearing in from every direction: rivalry among existing competitors, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitute products, and the bargaining power of both suppliers and buyers. When most of these forces are strong, they squeeze margins and make the industry a tougher place to make money; when they're weak, incumbents tend to enjoy healthier profits.

cards.q: What is the BCG matrix?
cards.takeaway: The BCG matrix sorts products by growth and market share into stars, cash cows, question marks, and dogs.
cards.a: The BCG matrix plots a company's products or business units on two axes, market growth and relative market share, to sort them into four categories: stars (high growth, high share) are worth continued investment, cash cows (low growth, high share) generate steady cash with little need for reinvestment, question marks (high growth, low share) are uncertain bets that need cash to prove out, and dogs (low growth, low share) are usually candidates to divest. It's a quick way to decide where to keep investing, hold steady, or cut loose.

cards.q: What does “economies of scale” mean?
cards.takeaway: Average cost per unit drops as production volume rises, letting big companies price lower.
cards.a: Economies of scale is the tendency for a company's average cost per unit to fall as it produces more. Fixed costs, like a factory or corporate overhead, get spread across a larger number of units, and higher volumes often let a company negotiate better prices from suppliers too. It's a big reason large companies can often compete on price in ways smaller rivals simply can't afford to match.

cards.q: What is opportunity cost?
cards.takeaway: Opportunity cost is what you give up by not choosing the next-best alternative.
cards.a: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option you give up when you make a choice. It matters in business decision-making because the real cost of any decision isn't just the money spent on it, it's also whatever else that same time, money, or resource could have produced instead.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a company’s mission and its strategy?
cards.takeaway: Mission is why a company exists; strategy is how it competes to get there.
cards.a: A mission statement explains why an organization exists and what it's fundamentally trying to achieve, while strategy is the specific plan for how it will compete and allocate resources to accomplish that. Mission tends to stay fixed for years or decades, while strategy adapts as markets, competitors, and conditions change.

cards.q: What is vertical integration?
cards.takeaway: Vertical integration means owning more of your own supply chain, upstream or downstream.
cards.a: Vertical integration is when a company takes ownership of additional stages of its own supply chain. Backward integration means acquiring a supplier, moving upstream toward raw materials; forward integration means acquiring a distributor or retailer, moving downstream toward the customer. Companies pursue it to control costs, secure supply, or capture margin that would otherwise go to an outside partner.

cards.q: What is a competitive advantage, and what are Michael Porter’s three generic strategies for achieving one?
cards.takeaway: Porter's three routes to advantage: be the cheapest, be meaningfully different, or dominate a narrow niche.
cards.a: A competitive advantage is something that lets a company consistently outperform its rivals over time. cards.q: What does “economies of scope” mean, and how is it different from economies of scale?
cards.takeaway: Economies of scope save money by producing different products together, not just more of one.
cards.a: Economies of scope are cost savings a company gets from producing multiple related products together rather than separately, for example by sharing R&D, distribution, or manufacturing capacity across product lines. It's a different lever from economies of scale, which comes from producing more of the same thing rather than a wider mix of things.

name: Accounting Fundamentals
description: Debits, credits, and how the books actually get built.
intro: Accounting is the record-keeping system behind every financial statement, and understanding it, even at a basic level, makes everything else in finance click into place faster. This deck starts from the actual mechanics: what double-entry bookkeeping means, how debits and credits work, and how the books get built up from a single transaction. It is written for someone who has never taken an accounting class, not as a shortcut around learning it, but as a clear first pass.

cards.q: What is double-entry bookkeeping?
cards.takeaway: Every transaction hits two accounts of equal value, so the books always stay in balance.
cards.a: Every transaction gets recorded twice, once as a debit and once as a credit, always for the same amount. That's what keeps the accounting equation, Assets = Liabilities + Equity, in balance no matter how many transactions pile up. It also builds in a natural error check: if total debits and credits ever stop matching, you know something was recorded wrong somewhere.

cards.q: What do “debit” and “credit” actually mean in accounting?
cards.takeaway: Debit means left, credit means right — which one grows an account depends on the account type.
cards.a: Debit and credit aren't inherently "increase" or "decrease" — they just mean the left and right side of an account. What each one does depends on the account type: debits increase assets and expenses (and decrease liabilities, equity, and revenue), while credits increase liabilities, equity, and revenue (and decrease assets and expenses). Memorize which accounts move which way, and the rest of double-entry bookkeeping follows from that.

cards.q: What is a T-account?
cards.takeaway: A T-account is a quick sketch of one account: debits on the left, credits on the right.

cards.q: What is the difference between a journal entry and the general ledger?
cards.takeaway: Journal entries record transactions in order; the ledger re-sorts them by account.
cards.a: A journal entry is the raw, chronological record of a transaction: it shows exactly which accounts were debited and credited as the transaction happened. The general ledger then reorganizes those entries by account, pulling every transaction that touched "Cash" or "Revenue," for example, into one place so you can track that account's running balance. Think of the journal as the diary and the ledger as the filing system built from it.

cards.q: What is an adjusting entry, and why is it needed at the end of a period?
cards.takeaway: Adjusting entries true up the books so revenue and expenses land in the right period.
cards.a: An adjusting entry updates account balances at the end of a period to capture revenue that's been earned, or an expense that's been incurred, but hasn't been recorded yet — think accrued interest, or a prepaid expense that's now been used up. They're needed because plenty of transactions span multiple periods, and without them, revenue and expenses would land in the wrong period and distort the financial statements.

cards.q: What’s the difference between FIFO and LIFO inventory valuation?
cards.takeaway: FIFO sells your oldest inventory first; LIFO sells the newest — and rising prices make the choice matter.
cards.a: FIFO (first in, first out) assumes the oldest units in inventory get sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects older, typically cheaper, costs. LIFO (last in, first out) assumes the newest units get sold first, so cost of goods sold reflects more recent, typically higher, costs. When prices are rising, that difference shows up on the financials: FIFO tends to report higher profit and a higher inventory value, while LIFO reports lower profit but a smaller tax bill.

cards.q: What is depreciation, and why is straight-line depreciation the simplest method?
cards.takeaway: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life instead of expensing it all at once.
cards.a: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset, like equipment or a building, across its useful life instead of expensing the full purchase price the year it's bought, matching the expense to the years the asset actually helps generate revenue. Straight-line depreciation is the simplest version: it expenses an equal amount every year, which makes it easy to calculate and forecast, even though many assets really lose value faster in their early years than a straight line implies.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a contra account and a regular account?
cards.takeaway: A contra account runs opposite its partner account, shrinking it instead of growing it.
cards.a: A regular account moves in its natural direction — assets and expenses grow with debits, for example. A contra account is paired with a related account but moves in the opposite direction, reducing that account's reported balance instead of adding to it. Accumulated depreciation is the classic example: paired with a fixed asset account, it carries a credit balance and lowers the asset's book value on the balance sheet.

cards.q: What is the difference between capitalizing a cost and expensing it?
cards.takeaway: Capitalize a cost if its value lasts years; expense it if the benefit ends this period.
cards.a: Capitalizing a cost means recording it as an asset on the balance sheet and spreading it over time through depreciation or amortization, because it creates value beyond the current period — buying equipment, for instance. Expensing a cost means recording the full amount immediately on the income statement, because the benefit is used up in the current period, like office supplies. The choice affects both the balance sheet and how quickly a cost hits reported profit.

name: Financial Markets & Instruments
description: How stocks, bonds, and other instruments actually trade.
intro: This deck covers how stocks, bonds, and other financial instruments actually trade, the difference between where a security is first issued and where it changes hands afterward, and the basic mechanics behind the markets you hear about in the news. It is aimed at giving you enough grounding to talk about markets confidently in an interview, not at making you a trader. No assumed background beyond general curiosity about how finance works.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a primary market and a secondary market?
cards.takeaway: Primary market money goes to the company; secondary market money just moves between investors.
cards.a: In the primary market, a company sells brand-new securities directly to investors for the first time, an IPO being the classic example, and the company keeps the proceeds. In the secondary market, investors simply trade those already-issued securities amongst themselves, like on the NYSE or Nasdaq, and the issuing company isn't even a party to the transaction. Only the primary market actually raises new capital for the company; the secondary market just lets ownership change hands.

cards.q: What is an IPO?
cards.takeaway: An IPO is a private company's first sale of shares to the public, becoming publicly traded.
cards.a: An IPO, or initial public offering, is the process by which a private company sells shares to the public for the first time and becomes a publicly traded company. It lets the company raise capital from a much broader pool of investors, but in exchange, existing owners give up some ownership and the company takes on the disclosure and reporting obligations that come with being public.

cards.q: What is a bond’s yield, and how does it relate to its price?
cards.takeaway: A bond's yield and price always move in opposite directions.
cards.a: A bond's yield is the return an investor actually earns from holding it, and it moves inversely to the bond's price: when price falls, yield rises, because the same fixed coupon payments now represent a bigger percentage return on the lower price paid. Pay less for the same future cash flows and your return goes up; pay more and it goes down. This inverse relationship is one of the most fundamental mechanics in fixed income markets.

cards.q: What does a bond’s credit rating tell an investor?
cards.takeaway: Lower credit rating means higher default risk, so investors demand a higher yield.
cards.a: A credit rating, assigned by agencies like Moody's or S&P, is their estimate of how likely an issuer is to default on its debt. Ratings range from investment-grade at the safer end down to high-yield, or “junk,” at the riskier end. Because risk and return are linked, lower-rated issuers have to offer higher yields to compensate investors for taking on that extra default risk.

cards.q: What is the bid-ask spread?
cards.takeaway: The bid-ask spread is the gap between what buyers offer and what sellers demand.
cards.a: The bid is the highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a security, and the ask is the lowest price a seller is willing to accept; the difference between the two is the spread. A narrow spread usually signals a liquid market with plenty of active buyers and sellers, while a wide spread signals lower liquidity or more uncertainty about fair value.

cards.q: What is a market maker?
cards.takeaway: Market makers quote both sides of the market constantly, earning the spread instead of betting on price direction.
cards.a: A market maker is a firm that continuously quotes both a bid and an ask price for a security, standing ready to buy or sell at those prices at any time. That constant two-sided quoting is what supplies liquidity to the market. Their profit comes from capturing the bid-ask spread across that flow of trades, not from predicting which way the price will move.

cards.q: What is a derivative, and what are options and futures examples of?
cards.takeaway: A derivative's value comes from something else entirely; options and futures are the two classic examples.
cards.a: A derivative is a financial contract with no value of its own, its value is derived from an underlying asset, like a stock, commodity, or index. Options and futures are both derivatives, but they work differently: an option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a set price, while a futures contract is an obligation, both sides are locked in to buy or sell it at a set price on a set future date.

cards.q: What’s the difference between a call option and a put option?
cards.takeaway: Calls profit when the price rises above the strike; puts profit when it falls below it.
cards.a: A call option gives the holder the right to buy the underlying asset at a set strike price before expiration, and investors buy calls when they expect the price to rise. A put option gives the holder the right to sell at the strike price, and investors buy puts when they expect the price to fall. Either way, it's a right, not an obligation, so the holder can just let the option expire worthless if exercising it wouldn't be profitable.

cards.q: What is market capitalization?
cards.takeaway: Market cap is share price times shares outstanding, a company's total public equity value.
cards.a: Market capitalization is the total value of a company's outstanding shares, calculated simply as the current share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. It's the standard way to categorize company size, large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, and to compare the relative size of publicly traded companies at a glance.

name: Microeconomics & Market Structures
description: Supply, demand, and how competition shapes a market.
intro: Interviewers in business, strategy, and even product roles often lean on basic economic reasoning: supply and demand, how competition shapes pricing, what happens when a market has only a few players instead of many. This deck builds those ideas up from first principles, so if the words "market structure" currently mean nothing to you, that is exactly who this is for. The goal is to be able to reason through an economic scenario out loud, not recite a textbook definition.

cards.q: What does the law of demand state?
cards.takeaway: Higher prices mean people buy less; lower prices mean they buy more.
cards.a: The law of demand says that, all else equal, a higher price leads people to buy less of a good, and a lower price leads them to buy more, which is what gives the demand curve its downward slope. It happens because as something gets relatively more expensive, buyers shift toward substitutes that meet the same need for less.

cards.q: What is price elasticity of demand?
cards.takeaway: Elasticity measures how sharply quantity demanded reacts when price moves.
cards.a: Price elasticity of demand measures how much quantity demanded changes when price changes. Demand is “elastic” when a small price move causes a big swing in quantity, typical for goods with close substitutes, and “inelastic” when quantity barely budges even as price changes a lot, typical for necessities with few substitutes.

cards.q: What is equilibrium price?
cards.takeaway: Equilibrium is the one price where what buyers want to buy matches what sellers want to sell.
cards.a: Equilibrium price is the price where the quantity buyers want to purchase exactly matches the quantity sellers want to offer, so there’s no leftover surplus and no shortage. Graphically, it’s the point where the supply and demand curves cross, and real markets tend to drift toward this price naturally over time.

cards.q: What happens to equilibrium price and quantity when demand increases but supply stays the same?
cards.takeaway: More demand at every price pushes both the price and the quantity sold higher.
cards.a: When demand rises while supply stays put, the entire demand curve shifts to the right, and the new equilibrium sits at both a higher price and a higher quantity. That’s because more buyers now want the good at every price level, so sellers can charge more and still sell more units.

cards.q: What’s the difference between perfect competition and a monopoly?
cards.takeaway: Perfect competition has many price takers; a monopoly has one price setter.
cards.a: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products and no single one is big enough to move the market price, so each firm just accepts, or “takes,” the going price. A monopoly is the opposite extreme: a single firm is the entire market, giving it real control over price, which typically means higher prices and less output than a competitive market would deliver.

cards.q: What is an oligopoly?
cards.takeaway: A few big firms dominate the market, and each one watches the others' every move.
cards.a: An oligopoly is a market controlled by a small number of large firms, where one firm’s decisions, on pricing especially, directly affect the others and usually provoke a response. Airlines and wireless carriers are classic examples: a handful of players control most of the market in many countries, so they compete and react to each other closely.

cards.q: What is marginal cost, and why does a firm compare it to marginal revenue?
cards.takeaway: Keep producing while extra revenue beats extra cost; stop right where they meet.
cards.a: Marginal cost is what it costs to produce one more unit, and marginal revenue is what that extra unit brings in. A profit-maximizing firm keeps producing as long as marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, and stops right at the point where the two are equal, since pushing past that point would only shrink total profit.

cards.q: What is a barrier to entry?
cards.takeaway: Barriers to entry are whatever keeps new competitors from entering and challenging incumbents.
cards.a: A barrier to entry is anything that makes it hard for a new firm to break into a market and compete with the companies already there, think high startup costs, patents, strong brand loyalty, or economies of scale that let incumbents produce more cheaply than a newcomer could. The higher these barriers, the less competitive the market tends to be, with fewer firms holding more pricing power.

cards.q: What is consumer surplus?
cards.takeaway: Consumer surplus is the extra value buyers get for paying less than they'd have accepted.
cards.a: Consumer surplus is the gap between what consumers were willing to pay for a good and what they actually paid, added up across every buyer in the market. It represents the bonus value consumers walk away with, and on a graph, it’s the area between the demand curve and the market price line.

name: Marketing Fundamentals
description: The core concepts behind how products get positioned and sold.
intro: Marketing questions show up in more interviews than people expect, not just marketing roles, but general business and case interviews that touch product or strategy. This deck covers the core vocabulary and frameworks, like the four Ps, that give you a structured way to talk about how a product actually gets positioned, priced, and sold. Written for someone starting from zero, with an emphasis on frameworks you can actually apply to a real example on the spot.

cards.q: What are the “4 Ps” of marketing?
cards.takeaway: The 4 Ps are the four levers a company pulls to bring a product to market.
cards.a: The 4 Ps, or marketing mix, are Product (what you're selling), Price (what it costs), Place (where and how customers can get it), and Promotion (how you tell people about it). Every go-to-market decision falls under one of these four buckets, and getting them working together is what makes a launch land instead of falling flat.

cards.q: What does STP stand for in marketing strategy?
cards.takeaway: STP walks you from a broad, messy market down to one clear position in customers' minds.
cards.a: STP stands for Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning. Segmentation splits a broad market into groups that share similar needs, targeting picks which of those groups is actually worth pursuing, and positioning defines how the product should be perceived, relative to competitors, in that group's mind. Run through in order, it takes you from 'everyone' to a specific, ownable position for a specific audience.

cards.q: What is brand equity?
cards.takeaway: Brand equity is the extra value a name adds on top of what the product actually does.
cards.a: Brand equity is the value a brand name adds beyond the product's raw functional benefits: the premium customers will pay, the loyalty they show, and the trust they extend before they've even used it. Two nearly identical products can sell at very different prices purely because one has a name behind it that people already believe in.

cards.q: What is customer lifetime value (CLV)?
cards.takeaway: CLV is the total profit one customer is worth over the whole relationship, not just their first order.
cards.a: Customer lifetime value estimates the total revenue or profit a business can expect from a single customer across the entire relationship, not just their first purchase. Because it captures repeat purchases over time, it's the number that tells a company how much it can afford to spend acquiring a new customer and still come out ahead.

cards.q: What does AIDA stand for, and what is it used for?
cards.takeaway: AIDA maps the four stages a stranger passes through on the way to becoming a buyer.
cards.a: AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, and Action, the stages a customer moves through before they buy: first they have to notice something exists, then care enough to learn more, then want it specifically, then actually act. Marketers use it as a checklist for campaigns and messaging, making sure each piece of content moves people to the next stage instead of skipping ahead.

cards.q: What is market segmentation, and what are some common bases for it?
cards.takeaway: Segmentation splits one big, messy market into smaller groups that actually behave the same way.
cards.a: Market segmentation is the process of breaking a broad customer base into smaller groups that share similar characteristics or needs, so you can market to each group more precisely than you could to everyone at once. Common bases include demographic (age, income), geographic (location), psychographic (lifestyle, values), and behavioral (purchase habits, brand loyalty).

cards.q: What's the difference between B2B and B2C marketing?
cards.takeaway: B2B sells to a committee on ROI; B2C sells to one person on emotion and price.
cards.a: B2B (business-to-business) marketing sells to other companies, where multiple stakeholders typically weigh in and decisions hinge on ROI over a longer sales cycle. B2C (business-to-consumer) marketing sells directly to individual consumers, where decisions are usually faster and driven more by emotion and price than by a formal evaluation process.

cards.q: What is a value proposition?
cards.takeaway: A value proposition is the one-line answer to 'why should I buy this instead of anything else?'
cards.a: A value proposition is a clear statement of the specific benefit a product delivers to its target customer, and why that beats the alternatives available to them. It exists to answer the customer's unspoken question up front: why choose this over everything else competing for their attention and money?

cards.q: What is churn rate?
cards.takeaway: Churn rate is the percentage of customers you're losing each period, the leak in the bucket.
cards.a: Churn rate measures the share of customers who stop doing business with you over a given period, a metric subscription businesses watch closely because it's their clearest signal of retention. A high churn rate means you're losing customers faster than is sustainable, even while new signups make total revenue look fine on the surface, so growth and churn always have to be read together.

name: Operations & Supply Chain Management
description: How companies manage inventory, production, and the flow of goods.
intro: Operations questions test a different kind of thinking than finance ones: how a business actually moves inventory, manages production, and keeps a supply chain from breaking under pressure. This deck introduces the core concepts, like the bullwhip effect, through simple explanations first, building toward the vocabulary interviewers expect you to use fluently. No operations background needed, just a willingness to think about a business as a physical system, not just a spreadsheet.

cards.q: What is the bullwhip effect in a supply chain?
cards.takeaway: Small demand blips get amplified into big order swings the further upstream you look.
cards.a: A small shift in real customer demand gets amplified as it passes upstream, from retailer to distributor to manufacturer, because each link tends to over-adjust its own orders instead of passing the true signal along unchanged. Those small overreactions stack at every step, so by the time the signal reaches the manufacturer, a minor blip in real demand looks like a huge swing in orders, distorting what's actually happening at the register.

cards.q: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management?
cards.takeaway: JIT brings materials in only as production needs them, trading safety stock for leaner inventory.
cards.a: Just-in-time inventory management brings materials and components in right as production needs them, instead of stockpiling them in advance. That keeps holding costs and waste low, since there's little excess inventory sitting around. The tradeoff is fragility: with barely any buffer stock, a single disruption anywhere in the supply chain can quickly bring production to a halt.

cards.q: What is Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)?
cards.takeaway: EOQ finds the order size where ordering costs and holding costs balance out to the lowest total cost.
cards.a: Economic order quantity is the order size that minimizes total inventory cost, balancing two costs that pull in opposite directions: the fixed cost of placing an order, and the cost of storing the units once they've arrived. Order too little and you pay that fixed ordering cost too often; order too much and you pay more to store the excess. EOQ is simply the quantity where those two costs are lowest combined.

cards.q: What is the difference between a push and a pull production system?
cards.takeaway: Push production guesses ahead of demand; pull production only makes what's already been ordered.
cards.a: A push system produces to a forecast, building up inventory ahead of actual orders in the hope demand shows up to match it. A pull system flips that logic: production only kicks off once real customer demand actually appears, which is the thinking behind JIT and cuts the risk of building goods nobody ends up wanting.

cards.q: What is Six Sigma?
cards.takeaway: Six Sigma hunts down process defects using data, aiming for near-flawless, 3.4-in-a-million quality.
cards.a: Six Sigma is a data-driven methodology for shrinking defects and variability in a process, aiming for a quality level where only about 3.4 defects occur per million opportunities. Teams typically work through it using DMAIC, a five-step cycle: Define the problem, Measure current performance, Analyze the root cause, Improve the process, and Control it so the gains stick.

cards.q: What is lead time?
cards.takeaway: Lead time is the full clock from placing an order to actually having it in hand.
cards.a: Lead time is the total stretch between placing an order and actually receiving it, covering everything from processing and production to shipping. The shorter it is, the less safety stock a company needs to keep on hand to reliably meet customer demand, since there's less time for something to go wrong or for demand to shift in between.

cards.q: What is capacity utilization?
cards.takeaway: Capacity utilization shows what share of a company's maximum output it's actually using.
cards.a: Capacity utilization measures how much of a company's total production capacity is actually being used, shown as a percentage of the maximum possible output. Low utilization can point to inefficiency or weak demand, while very high utilization is a warning sign too: the company is close to its ceiling and at risk of bottlenecks if demand climbs any further.

cards.q: What is safety stock, and why do companies hold it?
cards.takeaway: Safety stock is the buffer inventory that absorbs surprise demand spikes or supply delays.
cards.a: Safety stock is extra inventory held beyond what's expected to be needed, acting as a cushion against uncertainty, like a sudden spike in orders or a delayed shipment. It lowers the risk of running out of stock, but it isn't free: it ties up capital and storage space, so companies weigh that cost against the protection it buys them.

cards.q: What is a bottleneck in a production process?
cards.takeaway: A bottleneck is the slowest station in a process, and it caps what the whole system can produce.
cards.a: A bottleneck is the single stage in a process with the least capacity, and it sets the ceiling on how much the entire system can produce, no matter how efficient every other stage is. Speeding up any other stage doesn't help, since output still can't exceed what the bottleneck allows. That's why improving a process usually starts with finding the bottleneck and fixing it first.
